title: The Canadian natural wonder created by a massive meteorite
byline: 1 hour agoShareSaveAdd as preferred on GoogleJen Rose Smith
excerpt: More than 200 million years ago, a 5km-wide meteorite smashed into modern-day Quebec. Now, this eerily perfect ring that's visible from space is part of an epic road trip.
content:
More than 200 million years ago, a 5km-wide meteorite smashed into modern-day Quebec. Now, this eerily perfect ring that's visible from space is part of an epic road trip.

Rain pelted my windshield as I steered northwards through the boreal forests of Quebec. Black spruce and balsam firs wove a dense tunnel around the road, and the sky was a low mass of clouds.

Behind me was the windswept coast of the St Lawrence River. Hours ahead lay an unblinking eye that gazes skyward – one so vast it's visible from space. Seen from above, the 72km (45-mile) wide Manicouagan crater forms an eerily perfect ring of water; mountains rise from its centre like a dusky pupil, while rivers and tributaries vein outward from the lake, vanishing deep in the woods.

Manicouagan – AKA: the "Eye of Quebec" – is one of the planet's best-preserved impact craters, created by a 5km- (3-mile-) wide meteorite that threw debris as far as Japan and may have wiped out entire pelagic ecosystems some 214 million years ago. Only when astronauts' photographs from space eventually appeared in 1983 did its vast scope become visible.

Until the 1960s the region surrounding the crater was roadless, but these days, you can drive there on a partially paved rural highway that forms the start of the 1,700km (1,056-mile) Expedition 51 road trip across Quebec and Labrador via the Trans-Labrador Highway, so named for the latitude it follows.

"For Québécois, driving to Manicouagan is the dream," said one local, whom I'd met earlier that summer near the US border. "If you're going, you need two things: a reliable four-wheel-drive truck and clear weather."

This was sensible advice. Yet by the time I filled up my aged and rusting Prius, a huge storm had formed in central Canada and was gaining momentum on an eastbound run. The satellite map showed violent rain showers barrelling directly towards Manicouagan. But it was summer and the eye was calling, so I left my home in Vermont and headed north.

From whales to dams

The road to Manicouagan is Quebec Route 389, a two-lane sidewinder that begins in the city of Baie-Comeau on the north shore of the St Lawrence River. To get there I followed the river's coastline north-east 420km (261 miles) from Quebec City, a scenic drive known as the Route des Baleines (Whale Route).

As I drove, I scanned the water for some of the 13 species of cetaceans found in the St Lawrence River during its May-to-October whale-watching season – from slim harbour porpoises to immense blue whales. Standing on the free car ferry across the Saguenay River, I spotted an unmistakable flash of white.

At Baie-Comeau, I stopped to explore pink-streaked rock formations at Boisé de la Pointe St-Gilles park. Rosy snakes of feldspar wiggled across its waterfront slabs of dark-grey granite, which slope to the river's tidal flat.

The rain started gently as I turned north on Route 389, winding through S-turns to the hydroelectric dam Manic-2. In the summer months, the Hydro-Québec-operated facility – along with the bigger Manic-5, upstream – opens to the public for free guided tours.

Four dams were built on the Manicouagan River in a project that stretched from 1959 to 1970, my guide explained, as we walked through its growling inner workings. When water backed up behind the dams, the Manicouagan impact crater began to fill with water that swirled around the mountainous rise at its centre, creating the "eye" of water that's now visible from space.

"It took nine years for the crater to fill," the guide said, as we discussed the immense earthworks, blasting and engineering the barrages required.

Another 191km (119-mile) drive further to the north, mud-spackled trucks filled the car park at Manic-5, the world's largest multiple-arch-and-buttress dam, whose elegant concrete face seems to defy its massive scope.

I stopped for my second dam tour of the trip. In the surrounding valley, I learned, a temporary city sprang up in the 1960s to house workers, who harnessed the force of entire river systems. In the dam's small museum, I saw images of their families playing in the snow, heading to church, drinking at social halls. The project also brought roads here – including the one that would become Route 389.

Into the land of the Innu

"They did many things to build the dams, but what they did not do is ask the Innu first," said Céline Bacon, cultural and tourism officer for the First Nations Innu community of Pessamit, whose traditional territories include those covered by the reservoir.

Plan your visit:

Best time to visit: Snowmobilers and truckers journey to Manicouagan in the winter, but summer and autumn bring the best road-trip conditions. The Manic-2 and Manic-5 dams are open for tours from mid-June to the end of August.

What to do: Bring your own boat or paddleboard to explore Manicouagan Reservoir. Or, walk one of the trails into the nearby Monts-Groulx mountain range – like the 7km (4.3-mile) round-trip hike to the summit of Mont-Harfang.

Where to stay: Facilities at Manicouagan are limited. Relais-Gabriel at the crater's south-eastern edge offers very basic rooms and meals; the Innu-run Station Uapishka has a shoreline lodge, camping and meals.

The rain turned to a torrent as I continued north; dense stands of boreal forest crowded the edge of the road. For countless generations before the roads were built, Bacon explained, Innu people travelled on foot and by canoe into this landscape, returning each year to seasonal hunting and fishing camps.

"The dams transformed our territory, broke the ways we hunted and fished and gathered," said Bacon, who was raised on family stories of life on the land surrounding Manicouagan. "You can still see some of the old portage routes. My mother talked about them by name."

Rising waters weren't the only rupture. Beginning in the 1950s, Bacon said, the Canadian government increasingly forced Innu families to send their children to government schools, making traditional livelihoods impossible. "With that change, we lost so much of what we knew."

Out of the car and into the eye

After visiting the dams, many travellers head south back to Baie-Comeau. Others go much farther north, following Route 389 to join the Trans-Labrador Highway to Labrador City.

"We've been planning this for years," said one visitor, from British Columbia, who was bound for the end of the road. He'd waited for retirement before tackling the journey. "When else do you have time for the Trans-Labrador?"

Compared with such trips, my own tempestuous, 11-hour drive from Quebec City to Manicouagan seemed restrained, an epic journey writ small. Yet when I caught my first glimpse of the rain-swollen reservoir, I was thrilled by my final destination.

A passing astronaut would have glimpsed only a thick quilt of fog; around me, saturated evergreens slumped, heavy with rain. I couldn't see much of the crater, but even through the mist the lake – the heart of Unesco's Manicouagan Uapishka Biosphere Reserve – conveyed enormous space and silence.

Scraping grit from boots sodden from that afternoon's hike to nearby Mont-Provencher, I checked into Station Uapishka, a lakeside research station and lodge operated by the Innu of Pessamit and co-founded in partnership with the Unesco reserve. Inside, I met Innu chef Simon Landry-Asselin, who prepares meals at the lodge using ingredients that he forages from the surrounding forest, like spruce tips and the aromatic leaves of Labrador tea, an evergreen shrub.

"This lodge is our chance to share some of who the Innu are with visitors," he explained. "It's my chance to share the ingredients that our ancestors have always known." That night, I dined on baked cod topped with fireweed blossoms Landry-Asselin gathered in the nearby mountains, as wet gusts buffeted the windows.

Yet the next morning, I woke to skies washed clear of clouds. When I walked to the edge of the water, I could see the dark summit of 952m (3,123ft) Mont-Babel, the mountain that formed at the centre of the crater when bedrock violently rebounded following the meteorite's impact. The water had stilled to a glassy mirror.

Tucked in the back of my muddy car, my balled-up paddleboard had seemed faintly comical at the height of the storm. On the shores of Manicouagan I inflated it, then pushed off into the water, hugging the bays and promontories of its shoreline.

When the lodge disappeared behind me, all traces of people vanished – once again, I imagined the lonely view from space. But I had come to know this wilderness as a human one. Far below the lake's surface were the drowned ancestral hunting camps, the trails that the Innu of Pessamit once walked on their seasonal journeys.

As I paddled, sun illuminated beaches at the water's edge. A bald eagle squawked from a nearby rock. The water stretched away towards both horizons in a shining arc, bright and blue as an open eye.

--
